title: USA unveils 2026 World Cup kits, featuring waving flag and metallic star imagery
content:
U.S. Soccer and Nike on Monday released the jerseys and full kits that the U.S. men’s national team will wear at the 2026 World Cup.

The home kit evokes the American flag, with wavy red-and-white stripes running horizontally across the jersey.

The away kit — which multiple players have said is their favorite — is a dark “obsidian” color with metallic stars.

The stars are hardly visible from afar but more noticeable up close, and reflective from certain angles. “You see it on the pitch, and then you see it close up, it’s [almost] two different kits,” Maribeth Towers, U.S. Soccer’s VP of consumer products, told The Athletic.

Both kits are the product of extensive discussions, including with USMNT players, who mostly disliked their 2022 World Cup kits and pushed U.S. Soccer and Nike for more involvement in the 2026 process.

Some players even resisted a photoshoot in the 2022 kits, which were a simple white jersey and a blue tie-dye design. “That,” midfielder Tyler Adams told The Athletic and two other outlets, “started the conversation: next time around, let’s have a say.”

This time, a dozen players were interviewed at the onset of the process. Some were given the opportunity to sample fabrics and give Nike’s design team their opinions on various colors, textures and patterns. Then, last June, they were shown proposed designs, and asked for a “re-do” of the away kit, Towers and others said.

“We decided to go navy blue with silver stars, which I think represents us perfectly,” Adams said. “I think that’s gonna be an all-time classic jersey.”

The approach to the two kits, U.S. Soccer and Nike directors said, was to design one that was overtly, “undeniably American” and another that was more subdued.

“We wanted to make sure that the home [jersey] was very wild and obvious,” Yazmin Rosete, one of Nike’s lead designers, said at a kit launch event earlier this month. They wanted something that would instantly catch players’ eyes when they looked up into World Cup stands this summer.

Several players specifically advocated for some iteration of the “Waldos,” the 2012 USMNT kits with red-and-white horizontal stripes. Nike, though, wanted to avoid “any retro imagery.” U.S. Soccer agreed. “What we didn’t want to do is take a look backwards,” Alyssa Chargar, U.S. Soccer’s senior director of licensing, told The Athletic.

Their solution was the waviness. “The motion of the flag,” Chargar said, “was key for us.”

“The away [kit],” Rosete said, “is more of that on-and-off-pitch look, more lifestyle.”

That was the players’ request. Their message, according to Ronnie Stewart, a global football product director at Nike, was: “We just want something we can wear to the club.”

Towers recalled that, upon seeing the final design, one player said with approval: “Yeah, that’s perfect, you could wear that to a bar with your friends on a Friday night with a pair of jeans.”

Stuart McArthur, a senior director at Nike, told The Athletic: “We had a ton of different options. But [the final design] came from pure athlete insight. They wanted to feel cool. They wanted to feel energy, and they wanted to feel that intimidation factor of having the dark kit.”

Some players wanted a “bad-ass black” kit, Towers said. The dark “obsidian” look was essentially a compromise between black and navy blue.

And it was a compromise between a desire for stars and the desire for something stealthy or subtle.

“On the dark kit, the silver is sort of a reflective silver,” Adams said. “I think that was one of the cool pieces we wanted. You can’t really see from certain angles how the stars pop. And then in person, when you’re at a certain angle, the light reflects a certain way off of it, and it’s kind of shining, like chrome, which is kind of cool. I think that’s something that makes that kit really unique. And for me, that’s my favorite one.”

The bigger-picture goal was to create not just a kit but a nascent identity.

“You look through the [history of] U.S. national team kits, there’s not a lot of consistency,” McArthur said. “And that’s a cool thing. In the past, we’ve gone after lots of different looks. … But I think there was a feeling, and is a feeling, that there’s an opportunity to maybe have a little bit more consistency about what the U.S. national team kit looks like.”

Adams agreed. “The U.S. jerseys change every year so drastically,” he said. What he, the federation and Nike wanted was, essentially, to create an American equivalent of Holland’s orange or Brazil’s yellow.

“We want to try and etch our way into [having] at least one that always has stars, or always has stripes,” Adams said. “Because that’s the U.S.”

The USMNT will debut the new jerseys this month against Belgium (March 28) and Portugal (March 31). Those friendlies are the last two before head coach Mauricio Pochettino names his 26-man World Cup squad in late May.
